title: More Modular Exponential (MODP) Diffie-Hellman Groups for IKE
summary: Defines new Modular Exponential Diffie-Hellman groups for the Internet Key Exchange protocol. It documents the already widely used 1536-bit group 5 and adds larger groups numbered from 14, with sizes up to 8192 bits, and explains how the primes were chosen. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IKE peers use a Diffie-Hellman group during key exchange. RFC 3526 standardizes one previously used group and defines five larger groups that peers can select from.

questions: what are the ike modp groups
how big should a diffie-hellman group be
subtitle: Six named prime groups for the Diffie-Hellman operation used by IKE.

tldr.problem: IKE's original Diffie-Hellman groups were estimated to provide strength comparable to a symmetric key of 70-80 bits. Stronger encryption options called for larger groups.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3526 standardizes the previously used 1536-bit group 5 and defines five groups with moduli from 2048 to 8192 bits. Each group specifies a prime and generator 2.
tldr.outcome: IKE implementations can negotiate from a shared set of larger groups. The RFC does not assign groups to particular AES key sizes because strength estimates differ.

today: RFC 3526 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2003. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IKE Needs Additional Groups
sections.content:
Internet Key Exchange (IKE) negotiates a Diffie-Hellman group for certain cryptographic operations. IKE originally defined four groups, which this RFC describes as approximately as strong as a symmetric key of 70-80 bits.

RFC 3526 defines larger groups for use with stronger encryption. It does not say which group should be paired with each AES key size because published estimates of the required group sizes disagree. It also does not define a group larger than 8192 bits, which the RFC says would be too slow for practical use on hardware of that time.
sections.plainLanguage: IKE needed larger Diffie-Hellman groups for stronger encryption options. The RFC offers several sizes without prescribing which one to pair with a particular AES key.

sections.title: The Six MODP Groups
sections.content:
The RFC documents group 5, a 1536-bit group that had been used by implementations but was not defined in RFC 2409. It standardizes that existing assignment. Groups 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 use moduli of 2048, 3072, 4096, 6144 and 8192 bits respectively.

For every group the RFC gives a prime in a mathematical formula and in hexadecimal, and specifies generator 2. Implementations use the assigned group identifier to select the same parameters during IKE negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines groups numbered 5 and 14 through 18. Each group has a specified prime and uses generator 2, so peers can select matching parameters.

sections.title: Choosing the Secret Exponent
sections.content:
The group is only one part of the Diffie-Hellman calculation; the secret exponent must also be large enough for the system's intended strength. The RFC says the exponent should not be the weakest link and should have double the entropy of the strength of the whole system.

For example, if the system uses a group estimated at 128-bit strength, the exponent must use more than 256 bits of randomness. The RFC does not give a group-to-AES mapping, so implementers must select parameters that fit their security requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: A large group does not compensate for a weak secret exponent. The RFC says the exponent needs enough randomness to match the strength expected from the system.

sections.title: Security Estimates Are Ranges
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that group-strength estimates depend on the method used. It provides estimates from both ends of a range and says the actual estimate is likely to lie between them.

For group 14, with a 2048-bit modulus, the two estimates are 110 and 160 bits. For group 18, with an 8192-bit modulus, the estimates are 190 and 310 bits. The table also gives minimum exponent-size guidance corresponding to each estimate.
sections.plainLanguage: Security strength is an estimate, not a precise measurement. The RFC gives two estimates for each group to show the range of possible assessments.

sections.title: Assigning Additional Group Numbers
sections.content:
IKE already defines groups numbered 1 through 4. RFC 3526 adds group 5 and groups 14 through 18. Requests for further group assignments use the IETF Consensus process described in RFC 2434.

The RFC expects new groups to be documented in a Standards Track RFC. This gives implementers a published specification for the group parameters associated with each assigned number.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC assigns identifiers to six groups. Adding another group requires IETF agreement and a published Standards Track specification.
